headline: High BMI projected to be only asthma risk factor with rising burden to 2050
dek: A Global Burden of Disease analysis in npj Primary Care found asthma burden linked to smoking, NO₂ and occupational exposure fell between 1990 and 2021, while high BMI is forecast to rise.
body:
Asthma burden attributable to most major risk factors declined worldwide between 1990 and 2021, but high body mass index (BMI) is projected to become a growing contributor by 2050, according to a study in npj Primary Care. The post on X was shared by the Respiratory Medicine Portfolio.

The researchers used Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 data to estimate asthma disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and age-standardised DALY rates (ASDRs) attributable to high BMI, smoking, occupational exposure and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) pollution. They examined links with the Socio-demographic Index (SDI) and used Bayesian age-period-cohort modelling to forecast to 2050. Data from 1990 to 2010 served as the training set to backtest trends for 2011 to 2021.

Smoking-related burden fell most sharply. The ASDR dropped from 41.95 per 100,000 in 1990 to 16.19 in 2021, a fall of 61.41%. NO₂ pollution and occupational asthma burdens fell by 48.45% and 45.57% respectively. High BMI showed the smallest reduction, at 21.99%, and the burden increased in low-middle SDI regions.

ASDRs for high BMI, occupational risks and smoking correlated negatively with SDI. The NO₂ ASDR showed a significant positive correlation with SDI (ρ = 0.56, P < 0.001).

The model projects the high-BMI ASDR will rise from 39.42 per 100,000 in 2021 to 53.79 by 2050, an increase of 36.45%. The authors concluded that high BMI poses a growing threat with significant regional disparities, and that future strategies should be tailored by SDI region and high-risk population, prioritising surveillance and intervention for high BMI.
key_quote: high BMI is projected to be the only risk factor with a continuously rising burden
